BUSINESS OF SUPPLY ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 63-PRICE OF GASOLINE
speechtext:
That this House demands that the Government instruct Petro-Canada and its retail outlets to reduce their prices at the pump by six cents a litre, a move which would enable Petro-Canada to fulfil one of its basic purposes which is to provide Canada with reasonable energy prices.
He said: Thank you very much, Mr. Speaker, for allowing me to lead off in this very important debate, which at the moment is a major issue in the country. It is an issue which the Government is going to hear more and more about as there is a tax and consumer revolt out there in the country. Members will soon, if not already, be inundated with letters, telegrams saying, "Enough is enough", and that "the price of gasoline in Canada has gone too high".
Canadians are paying too much for gasoline at the pumps and for their home heating oil. The world price of oil is dramatically declining, but Canadians are being hosed at the pump. This Government, led by the present Energy Minister, is doing absolutely nothing about it. It is simply the friend of the big oil companies. It has forgotten the Canadian consumer. I say to the Government it forgets the Canadian consumer at its peril. Oil prices have come down 30 per cent since December 6, 1985; from $29 U.S. a barrel to $20 U.S. a barrel on January 28. Prices are even lower than that and still falling, and Canadians know that. Those who live close to the border can drive across and see that prices on the American side are dramatically lower. Contrary to what the Minister of Energy told me and this House last March, they can see that world oil prices are not being passed on. The decline is not being passed on to Canadian consumers.
In the Halifax Chronicle-Herald, January 28, Jim Meek, a very good energy reporter in the country, wrote about an application that was made to the Public Utilities Board there; it is the only jurisdiction in Canada where oil companies have to apply to increase their gasoline prices. I will quote what he says:
Milton Veniot, lawyer for the provincial Government, told the PUB that world oil prices have declined 35 to 40 per cent ($15 per barrel) in the past few weeks. A figure he said was equivalent to 9.4 cents a litre at the pumps.
A Shell Canada official, however, said outside the hearing that the actual figure is closer to 8 cents a litre.
Shell Canada is saying there is a decline in world oil prices which equals at least 8 cents a litre. We are saying in our motion today there should be a 20 per cent drop in pump prices. This is done by lowering the wholesale price by about 20 per cent. Right now the wholesale price of a litre of gas is about 30 cents. Therefore, it should be lowered by 6 cents a litre, and that is the figure in our motion.
The Minister of Energy has said, "Yes, it will take time to pass through the system". There have been cartoons to that effect in The Toronto Sun. "It will take time for it to pass through the system as we have a market system, and it will take time for these dramatic declines to pass through the system". This is tremendously naive on the part of the Minister of Energy. She just does not understand. In my submission that is not the way the industry works. The Government should know this.
There is a very famous report called the "Bertrand Report" done by the Director of Investigation and Research of the Combines Investigation Branch. It is entitled "The State of Competition in the Canadian Petroleum Industry". It was published about four or five years ago. Mr. Bertrand says, and I quote at page 19 of the first volume, right at the beginning:
In the 1958 to 1973 period, the majors-
Meaning the major oil companies.
-consistently used monopolistic practices to restrict competition from the independent sector and to impose the billions of dollars in excess costs on Canadians.
If you look at the way our oil industry works and at the Government's own studies you will see that this is what is called a classic oligopoly, it is non-competitive.
The pump does not immediately reflect declines in the market. I think the Minister is naive, at best, and at worst she is misleading us on this matter. Prices will not go down dramatically right away for two reasons. First, the Government is piling taxes onto the consumer at the pump and second there is an uncompetitive industry.
I looked at the price of gasoline in the Minister's own riding of Vancouver Centre, which is adjacent to my riding of Vancouver-Kingsway. When the Conservative Government took power in September, 1984 the price of gasoline was about 50 cents per litre. In January, 1986 the price was 56.2 cents per litre. Of that increase, about 2.4 cents was in taxes and about 3.8 cents went to the oil companies. We are faced with a combination of the Government increasing taxes and the oil companies increasing profits. The consumer is being hosed at the pump.

To be more specific regarding taxes, since the Conservatives took power, the Government first increased the federal sales tax on gasoline from 9 per cent to 10 per cent in October,
1984,	a carryover from the Liberal Government. Then the Government raised the excise tax on gasoline by 2 cents per litre in its May 1985 Budget and this took effect in September,
1985.	The Government then increased the federal sales tax again from 10 per cent to 11 per cent on January 1, 1986, and it has scheduled another increase for the excise tax to take effect January 1, 1987. At that time, there will be another increase of 1 cent per litre, also as a result of the Finance Minister's May Budget. The Government keeps piling on taxes at the pump and the provinces enter the picture after that. They tack on an ad valorem tax to the federal tax.
Motorists are saying that enough is enough. I and many of my colleagues have received hundreds and indeed even thousands of coupons from the Canadian Automobile Association saying that the cost of gasoline is discouraging both Canadian and U.S. tourism and damaging our economy, and that the high price is unfair to those who must use their cars to drive to work. They say that motorists are prepared to pay their share of the costs to help build and maintain the highways, but they think it has now become an inequitable tax burden. I agree with the Canadian Automobile Association. We must stop raising taxes at the pump.
In her defence, the Minister says that she needs the money because of the deficit and to pay for social services. There is some truth to that. Yes, the Government does need money to pay for social services. However, I would point to what happened last week in the House of Commons. The House passed Bill C-82 which phased out the petroleum and gas revenue tax to the tune of $5.3 billion up to 1990. The Government gave the oil industry $5.3 billion while telling the motorists at the pump that it needs their money to pay for social services. Why did the Government give all that money to a very rich and fat industry? When the Minister says that we need money for social services, I ask why she passed Bill C-82 which phased out the tax and gave such a great lump sum to the oil industry.
The Government says that we have to give money to the oil industry because it will create 300,000 new jobs. I took a good look at that figure. This is a capital-intensive industry which spends most of its money on equipment, much of it on foreign equipment, and not on job creation. Sure it creates some jobs, but that figure came right out of the brief of the Canadian Petroleum Association, the lobby group for big oil companies which makes submissions to the energy committees of the Senate and the House of Commons.
The Government and the Minister are patsies for the oil companies. It is very simple to be popular, as the Minister has been for the past 10 months, by giving money to the oil companies. However, we finally see that the result is that she is taking money out of the pockets of the motorists.
How poor is this poor oil industry? Imperial Oil just declared year-end profits last year of $680 million. For the last quarter of 1985 when oil prices were going down, its profit was $250 million, a record, up by $50 million for the last quarter.
This is outrageous because at the same time the consumer is being milked at the pump.
There is no guarantee that prices will go down at the pump as they drop dramatically at the world level. I would like to indicate why that is so. Yesterday, I phoned Mrs. Cora McAra. She and her husband operate what was once a Gulf station, now a Petro-Canada station at Gravenhurst. I will refer to the notes I made while I was talking to her over the phone. She said that Petro-Canada wanted to have a difference of four-tenths of a litre in price between self-serve and full-service. The McAras wanted two-tenths of a cent a litre because the station down the road had that price and they wanted to compete with it. They even offered to pay the difference out of their own pockets. Petro-Canada refused. The McAras have a contract on consignment so Petro-Canada can dictate prices. However, the contract also indicated that they should be competitive.
A few days later, Imperial Oil, the other station to which I referred, put its price down to 47.9 cents per litre, so the McAras said to hell with it and decided to follow that move since they had to remain competitive. What did Petro-Canada, the instrument of Canadian oil policy, or so we thought, do? It closed the pumps on these poor people.

speechtext: That's the free enterprise system.

subtopic: BUSINESS OF SUPPLY ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 63-PRICE OF GASOLINE
speechtext:
Yes, that's their system. There was a meeting between the McAras and Petro-Canada. Petro-Canada's representatives said that they were there to chastise and intimidate her. Petro-Canada said it was in the business of making money. If they lowered the price two-tenths of a cent here, the price would have to be lowered in other places and Petro-Canada did not want to do that. It said that this is the way it is going to be so the contract was terminated. The McAras will lose $50,000 because the contract was to go until May 1987. Mrs. McAra told me that lots of Petro-Canada dealers are in the same position. They are not happy because the price is staying high. That is the way Petro-Canada deals with ordinary Canadians and small business people.
The Conservative Government has directed Petro-Canada to act like a private-sector company. The Government is on the way to destroying Petro-Canada with its national policy. This is a perversion of what Petro-Canada was set up to do. Petro-Canada was set up to be a price leader. That is why I have put this motion before the House today. Petro-Canada should be taking the lead in getting prices down but that is not happening, and it could be happening.
I said earlier that this is not a competitive industry. I do not have time to go into detail, but let me say a few things about it. Government Members can refer to various restrictive trade practices hearings that have been going on for the last 10 years to learn why the industry is not competitive. There is the consignment sales trick, the example that occurred with Petro-Canada and the McAras. There is the fighting brands trick. That is simple. That is when the big oil companies form another oil company, pretend it is a small oil company and force small companies out of business or discipline independent
February 4, 1986

dealers. Third, there is the matter of special allowances which control how much gasoline the dealers receive. Finally, there are contracts that restrict sales and purchases. All of this appears in the Bertrand Report.
I looked at the situation in the United States and found that what Mr. Bertrand said in his report was true. He said that one of the problems we have in Canada is that those who refine and wholesale the gas and sell it to the retailers are all the same people because 80 per cent of the industry is controlled by four or five companies. These companies can squeeze out the independents and create an uncompetitive industry. In three states of the United States prices are lower. In those states, there is a law providing that the retailer, the wholesaler and the refiner must be different parties. That is called divestment. California is another state where there are low prices. The reason is that there is lots of refinery capacity there.
What does our Government do in Canada? I note that the Hon. Member from the Montreal area, the Minister of State for Mines (Mr. Layton), is following my speech. Let him tell me why the Government can close those refineries. [Translation]
Why did the Government of Canada close the refinery in the Montreal area? Because it would lead to higher gas prices, another increase, and again the consumer is the scapegoat of Conservative policies.

I just say that we in the NDP are fighting for those people in the east end of Montreal in order that their refinery will not be closed, and so that they will have some refinery capacity. We are doing this so that the prices will not be restricted again and put up by the big oil companies. That is exactly what the Conservative back-benchers were saying; and I am reminded of the words of the Hon. Member for Duvernay (Mr. Della Noce) who understands this.
The Government does not have to go as far as I suggest. It could just look at the report of the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission. The Director of Investigation and Research in his report to the Commission last fall made a number of recommendations. He said, first, that we should end consignment sales and special allowances. Second, he said that we should end restrictive covenants; and, third, that we should end exclusive dealings. That would work. I ask Hon. Members to consider the McAra situation in this regard. Instead of just having to deal with Petro-Canada, the Government could deal with other oil companies as well and they would not be locked into a contract. That is one way the Government could go, but it is not doing that.
There is another option the Government has, and my Leader, the Hon. Member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent) has said this in the House. Under Section 7(2) of the Petro-Canada Act, the Government could order Petro-Canada to reduce prices and be a leader, not a follower, as the Minister of
Supply
Energy, Mines and Resources (Miss Carney) has said. It could be a leader in terms of getting prices down for motorists. I heard the Minister of Energy say that this may be illegal. I cannot see that. The Government is a majority shareholder in Petro-Canada. In fact, it is the only shareholder. Surely, even the majority shareholders of Imperial Oil could order Imperial Oil to do certain things. It is clear that the Government has the power under Section 7(2) of the Petro-Canada Act.
Also, in this regard, I would ask, since when is reducing prices a form of price fixing? I do not think that follows. In fact, I think it is a red herring and a cop-out. The Government could do certain things.
I wish to conclude by saying that we have to be fair in the country. We have to look at the broad view as well. There is a big slump in world oil prices-in fact, a dramatic slump. What we are arguing is that the Canadian consumer should benefit from that slump. Of course, there will be a problem on the other side. People will ask; "What about the Canadian producer?" We in the NDP have never argued for a market price for oil. We do not think there is a real free market in oil when there is OPEC and a few large American multinational oil companies which basically control world market. One or the other group controls the world market.
What has happened by going to world market prices is that the Minister of Energy has taken an enormous gamble by deregulating the industry. That is to say if the price drops dramatically below $20 a barrel, and it goes down into the teens or low teens, then that will create a problem for the western producers. There may be a point where the price becomes too low, and I acknowledge that. I am not advocating that the consumer always receive benefits and that the price go down to the lowest possible price at the pump. We have to keep Canadian industry-and I underline the word Canadian-and small producers alive. We have to watch that situation, and I draw that to the attention of the House. The point is that right now the price of oil is inflated by at least six cents a litre and something has to happen. It is only fair that the consumer receive some benefit because the consumer has not been receiving any benefit from the Government at all.
The Minister of Energy looked weak last week in the House. The Government's energy policy was exposed for what it is. The Minister was great when she was giving money away to the oil companies, but neither she nor her Government has the guts to get in there and protect the Canadian consumer. The Government can do this by using Section 7(2) of the Petro-Canada Act. In fact, it can be a leader instead of a follower.
I say to the Government: This consumer revolt will force action later if no action is taken now. Do not wait for 60 or 90 days in an uncompetitive oil system. Use Petro-Canada now as a leader and force those prices down in order to give the consumer a benefit. In this way all Canadians, through lower interest rates, increased purchasing power, and so on, will benefit. That is the intent of my motion today.
Therefore, to summarize, my motion reads as follows:
That this House demands that the government instruct Petro-Canada and its retail outlets to reduce their prices at the pump by six cents a litre, a move which

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a couple of questions I would like to ask of my hon. friend from Vancouver-Kingsway. First, how did he arrive at the six cents a litre figure? Second, his leader, once he came back from a visit to Calgary where he supported some provincial NDP candidate, advocated a floor price for oil. All of a sudden he said that we have to help the oil companies now that the price of oil is dropping so fast. Can the Hon. Member tell us what that floor price should be set at? How will he explain to consumers, if the oil price were to drop below that, that they would not benefit from that drop?

Mr. Speaker, I thought I answered both of those questions in my speech. At the beginning of my remarks I cited the Shell lawyer who said that the price was actually about nine cents a litre too high. I said that there should be a 20 per cent drop in pump prices. I also said that this should be done by lowering the wholesale price by about 20 per cent. 1 said that right now I think the wholesale price is about 30 cents a litre. Therefore, I advocated that the price be lowered by about six cents a litre.
The association of petroleum marketers is somewhat of an authority on selling gas at the pump, and on refining. This group markets 15 per cent of the gas in Canada and it has said that gasoline is from five cents to six cents a litre too high at the moment for consumers. 1 invite the Hon. Member to drop across the American border and see what the prices are there.
With respect to the fairness doctrine, I said in my speech that it has always been the position of the NDP that we have not advocated a market price. The Minister of Energy and the Premier of Alberta have hoisted themselves with their own petard. They have been so keen on deregulating, which the Western Accord did, that they have exposed the industry, if the price falls through the floor. The price has not fallen through the floor yet, but it has gone down dramatically.
What 1 am advocating at this point in time, as I said in my speech, is that there should be a break for the consumers. The consumers have not received any break and they deserve one. It is only equitable and fair that they receive one. If we do not do something then those oil companies will just keep the price high. They are not going to put the price down. There will have to be pressure brought to bear on them. I did not advocate a floor price.

The Hon. Member recognizes that there will be a problem if the price goes through the floor. The Canadian industry will be in real trouble. We have not reached that point yet. That is what I was saying in my speech.
I remind the Hon. Member that he should read the Western Accord, which was written by his own Government. I do not
have a copy here in front of me. However, if he were to look at it he would find that it contains a clause which states something along those lines; it gives the Government the power to intervene if prices do get into real difficulty. I am simply saying that it is time to give the consumer a break. I have warned that to be fair in the future, if we see dramatically low prices, then we have to look at whether or not at that time the producer should be given a break.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources

The Hon. Member has been the energy critic for his Party for a fairly long period of time. One would think by now that would understand the industry a little. In his speech he mentioned that the prices started to come down in mid-December after the OPEC meeting on December 9, but they did not really fall dramatically until-in his words- January 28. He knows as well as anyone else-and he is being mischievous in saying that prices can drop immediately-that it takes time for that oil to come out of the ground, to be pumped to the refineries, to be refined and to get to the pumps. He knows that takes from six weeks to eight weeks, at least. With the dramatic drop in late January, those prices will not hit the pumps until late March. The Hon. Member knows that.
What the Hon. Member would like to see is the national oil company, Petro-Canada, drop its price and lose money. The Government then has to come along and subsidize it, meaning the taxpayer has to subsidize gas prices at the pumps. That is completely unrealistic.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member says 1 am being mischievous. That is an insult to all those thousands of Canadian consumers who are protesting these prices. I am making their argument today. The Hon. That is no magic number. I put it to you, Mr. Speaker, that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources the boss of the Parliamentary Secretary, is not quite so sure either. Why else did she send a Telex-after a lot of prodding-to the industries? It is because she, too, is a little worried that they are not going to lower the prices. Their past history is to scoop up as much profit as they can. Unless we put the pressure on them, they are not going to lower the prices. It is not a competitive system.
The petroleum marketers told me that Mr. Conrad, whom I mentioned, has said that if prices were to be reflected, we could buy refined oil in New York which would be six cents to ten cents a litre lower. It is only a hope and a prayer that those prices are going to come down. The only way they will come

down is if we keep the pressure on this Government and on the oil companies to get those prices down.

Mr. Speaker, I would suggest that the Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell) ought to be concerned about the fate of consumers of petroleum products.
I wonder whether the Government should have forced the company to price its products without consideration for the market place and whether the company should be subsidized to a degree.
In short, the suggestion of the Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway is that we ought to levy additional taxes to subsidize people who buy petroleum products.
How can he reconcile his call for a six-cent a litre decrease with higher taxes, because in fact he is recommending that the Government make up the difference? Does the Government not represent all consumers? Should the Government not Fill its coffers before redistributing the wealth? Higher expenditures mean a higher deficit, and I should think the Hon. Member knows full well we simply have to get a handle on that deficit if only because it is the only way to economic recovery.
So why would the Hon. Member not try to explain his theory on the basis of general economics rather than specific cases? How can the Hon. Member advocate unrestricted redistribution of wealth without asking taxpayers to ante up? I wish he would explain that.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to inform the House that I cannot support the motion put forward by the Hon. Member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell). I think the motion is well meant. All of us would like to see the consumers get a break at the gas pumps. But it is also misguided because it proposes a disastrous means
Supply
of achieving that end. In fact, the motion reflects a basic misconception on the part of both Opposition Parties that the Government of Canada should play the leading role in determining oil prices. The previous Government has a well documented history of interventionist policies.
The belief that Canadians can be sheltered from the effects of fluctuating oil prices was one of the cornerstones of the infamous National Energy Program. The NEP was hailed by the Liberal Party as the answer to all of Canada's energy problems. It was promoted as being fair to all Canadians. We were told that it would create opportunity in the industry and that it would ensure security of supply. But the reality did not live up to the promise. The NEP turned out to be one of the most damaging programs ever instituted by a Canadian Government. Under the National Energy Program, from October 1980 to this past year-less than Five years-the prices consumers paid for oil and gas and oil products rose by 80 per cent. Let me remind Hon. Members that it was the Liberal Government of that day which was setting the prices.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: BUSINESS OF SUPPLY ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 63-PRICE OF GASOLINE
speechtext: Aided by the NDP.

subtopic: BUSINESS OF SUPPLY ALLOTTED DAY, S.O. 63-PRICE OF GASOLINE
speechtext:
Quite apart from the impact on consumers, the NEP spelled disaster for the industry. Under its interventionist policies and excessive tax regimes, the oil and gas industry stagnated. Foreign investment left the country. The industry lost its confidence and energy became an arena for federal-provincial bickering. Indeed, it divided our country.
It is not the policy of this Government to interfere with the marketplace. We believe that markets operate most effectively when they operate free of the whims of politicians and the machinations of bureaucrats. We have taken steps to free up the oil and gas markets and we are not about to reverse that process by acceding to this ill-conceived motion which is before the House today. The Government of Canada would no more order Petro-Canada to reduce its retail prices than it would tell General Motors what to charge for its cars or tell IGA what to charge for its bread.
One of the very First things we did as a new Government was to give Petro-Canada a new mandate. We told it to operate in a commercial, private sector fashion. We told it, if it wanted money, to raise it itself, because the taxpayers' purse is closed. The corporation has since shown it can compete as a private sector entity. It took the initiative in purchasing GulFs downstream assets from Olympia and York using its own funds and borrowings.
We believe that Petro-Canada is and will continue to be an important player in Canada's energy industry. In many respects, it will be the leader, but it will be subject to the natural forces of the marketplace, as are private firms. This does not mean that we do not want lower prices for consumers. Indeed, we expect lower prices in the weeks and months ahead if the current world oil price slump endures.
The opposition does not have a monopoly on concern for the consumer. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Miss Carney) has written to the Chief Executive OfFicers of the oil refinery companies underscoring the expectation that

Supply
consumers will see the benefits of lower prices. However, we are not in the business of ordering price reductions by Petro-Canada or any other firm. The prices that consumers paid under the National Energy Program have increased by over 80 per cent. Our policies are designed to strike a best balance between the interests of producers and those of consumers. We would not be benefiting consumers in the long run by taking a role in setting prices. We would only be disturbing the otherwise smooth workings of the marketplace. By taking a hands-off approach we are ensuring that prices will drop in an orderly and realistic fashion. Prices in the coming weeks will reflect supply and demand, local competition, and the depletion of the existing stocks of higher-priced crude.
To fully appreciate why domestic gasoline prices have not declined with world oil prices, Mr. Speaker, you must understand a basic operating principle of the oil industry. Retailing oil and gas is not like retailing bread. You do not move it through your store in a matter of hours or days. Much of our crude oil is purchased months in advance. I believe that the industry standard is to have one to two months of crude oil and product in reserve. As a result, Canada's oil companies have large inventories that were purchased in November and December before world prices began to drop sharply. This gasoline has to be sold before the cheaper crude now being purchased can work its way through the system.
Even Hon. Members across the floor cannot expect oil companies to sell gasoline at a loss. If they do, they should expect all other industries with feed stock and product inventories to pass through the news, and I emphasize "news", of price cuts on raw material instantly. This would apply to many of our industries including farming. Canadians can expect to see lower prices at the pumps, Mr. Speaker. Exactly when will depend largely on how quickly they deplete existing stock of more expensive crude.
I assure Hon. Members that the oil companies are well aware of the Government's stand on pricing. On January 28 my colleague, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources sent telexes to the oil industry leaders telling them that the Government expects that consumers will benefit from crude oil price reductions. We are looking to industry to ensure that those reductions are passed on as soon as possible and we have no reason to believe that they will not be passed on.
I was surprised to read in press reports last week that the federal energy policy would have to be completely rewritten in the face of declining world prices. This would have been a typical response of the previous Government. With no confidence in ordinary Canadians, it would believe that the Government and the bureaucrats knew better than buyers and sellers. Quite to the contrary, our policies were developed to be flexible to the movements of the marketplace.
Price reductions have been anticipated for more than a year. We also anticipate that prices will begin to rise again in the early 1990s, about the time when many of Canada's megaprojects will come on stream. This is called long-term planning
and it is something that there was all too little of under the previous Government.
I said earlier that our policies were designed to benefit both producers and consumers. They are, in fact, benefitting all Canadians. The Atlantic Accord was our first important energy agreement. It set the tone for everything that was to follow. As Hon. Members know, the Atlantic Accord ended years of protracted federal-provincial disputes over offshore resources. In establishing joint management in the offshore it made Newfoundland an equal partner in Confederation and paved the way for the development of the promising Hibernia field. While the most immediate benefits will be in eastern Canada, Mr. Speaker, all Canadians will benefit from the Atlantic Accord. It was an important step in establishing security of future oil and gas supplies.
I have already discussed the positive aspects of deregulation of crude oil prices which we achieved in the Western Accord. These prices are now determined by the market and increases will work their way through the production, transportation, and refining system to the gas pumps. But the Western Accord also removed inordinate taxation and regulation of the oil industry, and substantially improved its investment prospects. Investment means jobs and job creation benefits all Canadians.
A report for BP Canada and Petro-Canada Resources by the Canadian Energy Resource Institute illustrates the significant impact of just one project that will expand, given the environment created by the Western Accord. The Wolf Lake oil sands project northeast of Edmonton is expected to produce 61 million barrels of oil at a rate of 7,000 barrels a day. Preproduction costs are $115 million and operating costs are estimated at $1.1 billion over the 25 year life of the project. Wolf Lake will generate approximately $2.2 billion in income for those 25 years. Seventy-one per cent of this will occur in Alberta and 15 per cent will occur in Ontario and Quebec. The project could create 22,000 person years of employment, 5 per cent in Alberta and 34 per cent in Ontario and Quebec. Most of those jobs would be created through the life of the operating phase of the project. For every dollar spent on the Wolf Lake project during construction and operation, another $1.25 will be generated and spent throughout the economy. Those are the facts and they prove that producers are not the only ones benefitting from the new federal energy policy.
Our new natural gas markets and pricing agreement also reflects the all-important balance between benefits for consumers as well as producers. As the Minister of Energy has said, it is an agreement under which all parties win. In keeping with our policy that Government has no role in determining prices, the natural gas agreement provides for price deregulation as of November 1, 1986. After that all sales will be negotiated directly between buyers and sellers. This is already happening in some cases.
Producers benefit from this approach because it widens their markets and enables them to compete free of Government constraints. Relaxed rules for exporting natural gas also open up the U.S. market to Canada's industry. Consumers are also big winners, Mr. Speaker. Today they are paying less for
February 4, 1986

natural gas as a direct result of this new agreement than they would have under the old regime. They can expect to benefit from a market characterized by competitive pricing and new suppliers.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, our new frontier energy policy promises long-term benefits for all Canadians. It frees industry from excessive taxation and regulation and establishes realistic and internationally competitive incentives for frontier exploration and development. This activity will trigger a new round of job creation and social and industrial benefits, and will eventually contribute to Canada's security of supply.
None of these benefits can be realized without investment from both foreign and domestic sources. Canada's oil and gas industry is regarded as an excellent investment, even in these days of declining prices. In fact, oil and gas investment intentions were up about $2 billion in 1985, more than 25 per cent over the previous year. The Petroleum Services Association of Canada has estimated that this investment has created more than 10,000 jobs in the energy sector alone.
A study done earlier this year for the Independent Petroleum Association of Canada illustrates the benefits of a $1 billion investment in upstream conventional oil and gas projects. According to the study by Woods Gordon, this investment generates secondary effects of up to $1.4 billion in the Gross National Product. It creates 30,000 person years of employment. These are jobs for Canadians, jobs for people who were hurt by the interventionist policies of the previous Government.
While 80 per cent of the direct spending would be in Alberta and Saskatchewan, 30 per cent of the total income generated and 33 per cent of the employment spin-offs will be in Ontario and Quebec.
Oil and gas development is only one component, albeit an important one, of the Government's over-all economic strategy. It is this strategy that has contributed 6.6 per cent in growth to Canada's GNP during the third quarter of 1985. In the 17 months since the Government was elected, more than 450,000 new jobs have been created. As our Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) has said, that accounts for nearly 1,000 jobs per day since September 4, 1984.
Productivity surged by 4.9 per cent in 1985. The Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development predicts that Canada's growth in GNP in 1986 will be second only to Japan and that its traditional first-place ranking in job creation will resume in 1986. Inflation is being held at the 4 per cent range. Business investment was up by an annual rate of 11 per cent in the third quarter of 1985. These facts illustrate very clearly how our policies are helping the average Canadian.
To those who criticize our energy policy as being weighted in favour of the producers, I can only say that all Canadians are benefiting now from our initiatives of the past months and they can expect to benefit a great deal more in the future.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my privilege to address this motion today, a motion which calls for the Government to direct Petro-Canada to institute a decrease of 6 cents per litre in the price at the pumps for retail gasoline. In doing so, I would like to address a myth that has been circulating in the House in recent days. I believe it is very important for us as members of the Opposition to expound on the reasons why gasoline prices should come down.
It was very evident from the speech made by the Hon. Minister of State for Mines (Mr. Layton) that the Government does not accept the fact that there are substantive economic reasons for the price of gasoline to fall. I am referring to the amazing statement made by the Minister of State for Tourism (Mr. Murta) to the effect that tourism in Canada is not affected by the price of automobile gasoline. Of course, it would be unparliamentary to attribute to the Minister improper motives for making that statement, and I cannot say that the statement is a variance with the truth because it is only, after all, a hypothesis. However, what I will say is that the statement was inaccurate, misleading and was totally at variance with the opinion of not only the best industry sources but the industry unanimously. It was at strong variance with
the opinions of the former Minister of State for Tourism and it has aroused an outcry in the tourism industry about the insensitivity of the Government to industry in general and to the tourism industry in particular. It has shown the Government's evident lack of attention and concern to the opinions of that industry and to the possible fate of those in that industry when confronted by this sort of intransigence and blinkered attitude on the part of the Government.
The Minister of State for Tourism said in the House that gasoline prices do not affect the intentions of U.S. tourists to travel to Canada. I might say that that is manifest nonsense. I have not heard one person in the industry tell me that gasoline prices do not affect the intentions of U.S. tourists to travel to Canada. Moreover, I have not heard the same Minister say in the House that the price of gasoline did not affect the intentions of Canadians to travel. We must remember that the majority of tourists within Canada are, after all, Canadians. While American vacationers make a very great contribution to our tourist industry, it is, after all, to Canadians who Canadian tourist attractions and operators must first appeal.
The statement made by the Minister of State for Tourism ran contrary to the opinions of the industry as sampled by his own Ministry. I would like to quote from an impressively titled paper prepared for the National Tourism Tomorrow Conference entitled Prices: Perception, Reality and Value for Money. This is the result of what the Progressive Conservative Government has termed its consultation. These are the numbers that were produced by the consultative process of which the Government speaks so highly when questioned. On page 6 of the report, under the heading Consultation Results, the following is noted:
There were 180 respondents to the consultation process who mentioned prices as the major problem. As well, comments about prices were often raised under another topic cited as the major problem.
Comments about high prices as a problem were distributed as:
Gasoline	37.2%
Alcoholic Beverages	29.4%
All Prices	27.8%
Accommodation	17.8%
Food	13.3%-
It is the opinion of the Canadian tourism industry as consulted by the Government, that the high price of gasoline is more of a problem for the industry than the prices of accommodation and food put together.
The tourism industry does itself credit by the fact that it has not been slow in raising this problem with the Government and in attempting to convince the Government that the industry does indeed know the factors in its economic equation that will affect the future of their industry. It would appear that the Government believes it knows better and that the industry itself has no business telling the Government what affects the industry's potential for success.
Pride of place in this effort must go to the Canadian Automobile Association which started a nationwide publicity campaign to condemn high gasoline prices and the very evident effort that the Government is making to keep gasoline prices
February 4, 1986

high. The Executive Vice President of the Canadian Automobile Association has said that the Government has ignored recommendations from groups such as his which have pointed out the very negative effects that high gasoline prices have on the tourism industry, the transportation sector and the economy as a whole. He went on to say that this self-inflicted uncompetitive positioning is costing Canadians billions of dollars in tourism revenues, tens of thousands of jobs, something of which a Government that talks of job creation should take note, and millions of dollars in investment opportunities.
The Canadian Automobile Association is not alone in raising this problem and pointing out that Canadian gasoline prices are about 30 per cent higher than U.S. gasoline prices at the pumps. If the Government does not take some action now, that margin will increase further, unless, of course, it lets the dollar drop clear through the floor.
This is causing serious damage to our auto tourism industry and many other transportation-dependent industries, said the President of the Canadian Automobile Association.
On the very day that the Minister responsible for Tourism- and I wish he were here to listen-rose in the House to say that gasoline prices were not a problem, he and I received a telegram from the Tourism Industry Association of Canada, which states in part:
The cost of gasoline and jet fuel has for the past few years placed Canada at a serious competitive disadvantage relative to the U.S.A. The current drop in the world price of oil will further reduce the pump price in the U.S.A. in 1986.
The telex goes on to state, and I will just quote portions of it:
It is essential that Canada's Federal Government take the leadership in conjunction with the provinces and oil companies in initiating action to bring the price of transportation fuels in this country into a more competitive position.
That is the very clear position being taken by the Tourism Industry Association of Canada, which is the prime umbrella organization for the industry in the country. It is signalling the Government exactly what is needed.
Leadership is something we have not seen from the Government with respect to gasoline pricing. We finally managed to drag out of the Minister of Energy, after a few days of her habitual stonewalling, that she would indeed at least make the effort to send a telex to the gas companies saying that she expected that they would do something about the price of gasoline. We have not seen the telex, so we can only assume that, of course, it was phrased in such polite and diplomatic terms-

I would really like to hear the Minister of State for Tourism speak in this debate. If the Government's program to continue high gasoline prices is not damaging, I would like to know what is damaging to the tourism industry, which has said unanimously that higher gasoline prices are damaging.
The Hon. Member for Northumberland (Mr. Hees) had the figures right approximately two years ago on February 8, 1984 when he said in this House:
If the money had been used to reduce the cost of gasoline at the pumps, it would have made Canada a far more attractive place for tourists to visit. Eighty-five per cent of our dollars from foreign tourists comes from Americans visiting Canada. Of these, 74 per cent travel by automobile.

The Government has given us an increase in the gas tax on three separate occasions, and there is another increase to come in January of next year. It seems that the deregulated environment cuts but one way. I would say that whether it be regulation or deregulation it should cut both ways.
I would like to offer a couple of quotations from this morning's newspaper. They happen to be from The Globe and Mail, which is an excellent Toronto newspaper. The headline is: "Oil prices tumble below $18 a barrel". The article states:

the Saudis can now basically set the market where they want to and that they are inclined to set it lower rather than higher.

Let it tell them it is not going to do anything about oil prices, it is not going to exercise any form of judgment, policy setting, discretion or direction or any form of what it so negatively calls "intervention" in the marketplace because it does not believe in it. subtopic: HEAVY OIL UPGRADER PROJECT-NEED FOR GOVERNMENT ASSISTANCE
HEAVY OIL UPGRADER PROJECT-NEED FOR GOVERNMENT ASSISTANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, conventional supplies of light crude oil from western Canada are gradually declining as the older oil fields such as Leduc and Redwater run out. To remain self-sufficient in oil supply we must encourage the exploration and upgrading of our oil sands and heavy oils. If we do not, we will be turning the clock back and will become increasingly dependent on foreign crude oil.
The proven reserves of oil in the oil sands and heavy oil areas of north eastern Alberta stagger the imagination. There are enough reserves to supply Canada's needs for 200 to 300 years. We have the technology to produce this heavy oil and bitumen but the oil must be upgraded to light crude to meet Canada's refining requirements.
Husky has proposed a heavy oil upgrader at Lloydminster and has requested assistance in the form of loan guarantees. The Government of Alberta and the Government of Saskatchewan have agreed to assist. The federal Government has yet to make a final decision.
May I remind my colleagues that without Government help the Syncrude project would have failed. Without Government help, the Alsands project did fail.
We must recognize that special incentives are essential for most large energy projects to proceed in today's uncertain world. The Husky upgrader is vital to our nation's security. We must not and cannot allow ourselves to become dependent on foreign oil and thereby be hostage to a foreign power.
I urge all Members of the House to support federal Government assistance for the construction of the Husky heavy oil upgrader.

subsubtopic: TASKS FACING NEW PRESIDENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the new president of Canada Post is appointed, he or she will have the monumental task of addressing a number of very serious problems. For example, the new president must make the corporation fiscally responsible by reducing the annual deficit of some $300 million. The president must also alleviate the labour unrest which is a major problem in some larger urban centres.
Furthermore, he or she must address some severe inequities which currently exist. For example, in my riding of Brandon-Souris some rural mail delivery routes are being dismantled, while other rural and town residents continue to pay an annual fee for the rental of their mail boxes at the local post office. This is a practice which they, understandably, believe to be discriminatory.
There are inequities as well in the cities, where thousands of mobile homeowners and new homeowners are not receiving home delivery even though some of the new homeowners reside on streets which already receive service.
It is imperative that these inequities be rectified. The new president must make the corporation one which is responsible and fair to all Canadians, both financially and service-wise, whether they live in rural or urban Canada and whether they live in older or newer sections of our cities.

Mr. Speaker, there is widespread concern about the Canadian dollar falling below 70 cents. There is much speculation as to the root causes. Clearly the sharp decrease in oil prices has a negative impact on producing countries such as Canada.
However, I would submit that the past decade of wild and irresponsible spending by the former Liberal Government is the root cause of our falling dollar.
The Right Hon. Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Turner) rants and raves about the falling dollar and rising interest rates, yet he was the father of the deficit.
It took Canada 100 years to create a national debt of $20 billion. It took the Liberals a mere 10 years, starting in 1974, to increase the national debt to almost $200 billion.
In the mid 1970s the annual deficit was $2 billion. In 10 years the Liberals had increased this to $36 billion.
Our new Conservative Government is acting in a responsible manner to reduce the deficit, and thereby to reduce the crushing impact of interest charges on that debt which now absorb one-third of our revenues. Further tough measures are needed over the next several years to reduce the deficit and to restore financial stability and confidence.
What we do not need is the self-righteous, hypocritical, political posturing by the Opposition. The situation is too serious for that.

subsubtopic: SUMMIT CONFERENCE-ABSENCE OF MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, why does the Government create a Minister of State for Forestry (Mr. Merrithew) and then hide him in the closet? Despite its professed concern with acid rain, the Government will have a delegation of only two officials plus a Parliamentary Secretary at the opening in Paris tomorrow of the first Summit Conference on the future of the world's forests.
The three day meeting is convened by President Mitterand and is being attended by representatives from 60 countries. Heads of State attending include Chancellor Kohl, the Prime Minister of Ireland, President Diouf of Senegal, Jacques Delors, President of the European Community, and Edourd Saouma, Director-General of the UN Food and Agricultural Organization.
Considering the significance of acid rain effects on Canadian forests and our vast forest resources, would it not be incumbent on Canada to have, as a minimum, the Minister of State for Forestry in attendance?
This is yet another indication of the priorities of the Government-if it has any-and its level of commitment to anything which does not relate to the deficit using archaic Tory bookkeeping mentality. Yet the state of our forests will very much affect the deficit about which the Government is so worried. Without healthy forests, we will see the deterioration and demise of one of Canada's major industries and a significant source of employment for many Canadians.
With these risks in mind, many people are asking why the Government showed so little interest, as demonstrated by the token representation Canada is sending to Paris.

If the Members on that side want to cry for the oil companies, they can do it, but I know the Canadian people will not cry about the poor state of the oil industry in this country.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 63-PRICE OF GASOLINE
speechtext:
The question of what constitutes a fair return was a question posed by my friend, the Parliamentary Secretary, but not properly responded to other than by an invitation to the Library. Members of the New Democratic Party may laugh when the Parliamentary Secretary says that the industry was taxed almost out of existence, but that is the truth. The fact is that before the National Energy Program, the record of the industry, whether multionational or Canadian owned, was that of a reinvestment practice of 105 to 110 per cent. It was the National Energy Program which discouraged that.
Last Saturday, as is my practice on a regular basis, I held a town hall meeting in my riding of Edmonton South. It was attended by a good many people. This particular town hall meeting was held in opposition territory, one of the four out of 176 polls which I lost in the 1984 election. I might add, it was NDP territory. We heard some very interesting questions at that meeting. One of the questions posed was the question related to today's motion, and that is, "Why aren't you lowering the costs to gasoline consumers by ordering Petro-Canada to cut its price by a fixed amount?" I had no difficulty answering that question nor did the 114 other people at that meeting including, I would submit, many New Democrats who thought it was the height of folly to suggest that we increase the deficit in order to deliver a lower price at the pumps.
My hon. friend, the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, has alluded to a very interesting editorial in last Friday's Ottawa Citizen, a newspaper which I do not always embrace but which 1 think has lucidly addressed this particular question. It is a newspaper which uses the expressions "the mouths of mock-furious Liberals and New Democrats" and "it is juvenile to expect that a downturn in world oil prices will be felt instantly at the gas pumps". The very idea that Petro-Canada should be manipulating prices is anathema to the people of Canada. Do we want Governments setting the price of bread, for example? That, I submit, is a Marxist, Third World concept.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 63-PRICE OF GASOLINE
speechtext: Ha!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 63-PRICE OF GASOLINE
speechtext: It is to laugh, is it?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 63-PRICE OF GASOLINE
speechtext: He wants the Government to set the price of bread.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 63-PRICE OF GASOLINE
speechtext:
Perhaps the Hon. Member would relish the idea of the Governor General's Foot Guards charging Parliament Hill.
It is a fact, and I think the record should show, that 80 per cent of the personal taxes paid in this country go toward paying interest on the Liberal-NDP debt which was inflicted upon the country. We have to put our house in order, and the very thought of putting more money into Petro-Canada in order to lower the price of gasoline is foolhardy, to understate the case.
Let us look at what the Government has done in order to benefit the development of that great engine of growth, the energy industry, over the past 17 months. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Miss Carney) has secured the Atlantic Accord, the Western Accord and its companion document, the agreement on natural gas markets and prices, and has introduced the new frontier energy policy, each of which go effectively toward eradicating the last vestiges of the infamous National Energy Program. These are formidable accomplishments considering that, when they are assessed as a group of policy initiatives, they have a great total effect. It is even more noteworthy that these agreements have been concluded with the interests of all regions of Canada in mind and therefore all consumers.
As Hon. Members know, the federal Government is committed to establishing a new Canadian economic environment free of excessive regulation and market intervention within which industry and commerce in all regions can flourish. Since the signing of the Western Accord just 10 months ago, the industry has announced an array of projects and plans that cumulatively will involve the investment of over $10 billion, directly employing more than 46,000 Canadians in construction and ongoing operations. Companies have announced their intentions to pursue a number of other projects pending conclusion of the detailed negotiations with Governments and prospective partners totalling another $12.5 billion and employing upwards of another 28,000 Canadians. Not included in these figures is the massive investment plan to develop the Hibernia
February 4, 1986

on the offshore of Newfoundland. Estimates here are that more than $5 billion will be invested with the creation of thousands of construction and ongoing jobs for Newfoundlanders and other Canadians.
The Government of Canada is well aware of the cyclical nature of oil prices and has designed its energy policy with that in mind. That is why we moved to market-sensitive pricing. As the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources said recently, we are well positioned to take advantage of both the upstream and the downstream in energy. Our energy policy is still one of the most competitive in the world and will withstand the test of changing prices.
There has been a lot of confusion about the impact of the recent decline in crude prices. I am pained, to paraphrase what the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) said on a different matter here in the House today, to say that it ill becomes the dignity of the office of Hon. Members to contribute to that confusion. I would like to try to sort it out for Hon. Members this afternoon. First, let us look at the upstream.
Many questions have been asked about the viability of major oil and gas projects in light of declining world oil prices. First, production of many of the major energy projects currently under construction will not commence until the mid-1990s. It is therefore not so much current price levels but the future of oil price movements that determines the economic viability of these projects. Most observers, and I think even the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North with his suggestion of $5 per barrel, would expect prices to rebound in the early 1990s, possibly increasing at rates above the inflation rate. Indeed, the very fact that the long-awaited drop in oil prices appears to be taking place now removes the doubt. The sooner this happens, the less doubt about the eventual rise.
We all hope that there will continue to be peace in the Middle East, but it is a fact of which none of us need to be reminded that if peace does not prevail in the Persian Gulf, for example, this oil glut could be a very transitory occurrence. In the unlikely event that prices remain depressed over the long term, the return on these major projects would obviously be affected. Nonetheless, many of the major energy projects can withstand a fairly significant drop in the world price. In particular, we could refer to projects such as Hibernia, the existing oil sands operations and the many in situ bitumen projects in Alberta.
A statement was made very recently by an executive of Imperial Oil to the effect that Imperial Oil's major resource projects, particularly the Cold Lake heavy oil development, are actually quite resilient to price erosion.
That is the upstream. What about the downstream which of course has a more immediate impact on the consumer? Again, I remind the House of the positive steps the Government has taken to enable consumers to benefit from the recent decreases in oil prices.
Through the Western Accord, we deregulated the price of crude oil and freed it from the previous Government's rigid pricing policies. Crude oil prices are now set by the market-
Supply
place. Under deregulation, Canadian crude oil prices respond very quickly to changing international market conditions. This process is evident today. The recent substantial declines in international crude prices have already resulted in lower posted prices for Canadian crude oil. There is no doubt that the Western Accord and deregulation have resulted in a very effective and responsive Canadian crude oil market. This cheaper crude will be refined into cheaper gasoline. However, first, this lower-priced crude must work its way through the pipeline system into the refineries. A barrel of light Canadian crude typically takes Five weeks to travel from Edmonton to Montreal. This industry operates like any other that stockpiles feedstock and products, such as the forest products industry and even farming. To say that lower oil prices should ignore inventories is to suggest that milk and bread should see an instant price drop as soon as farmers' own oil costs go down.
Furthermore, companies generally run down higher-priced inventories of crude and product before lowering prices to reflect their lower costs. These inventories, which cover from one to two months of requirements, are necessary to ensure that customers enjoy uninterrupted oil product supplies. I remind the House that it was the previous Government, the Liberal Government which prohibited companies from immediately passing through crude price changes to product markets. Instead, they were forced to wait until transportation lags and inventory draw-down had been accounted for. What we are saying is: Let the market decide-it could be sooner than the old rules would have allowed.
Once the companies begin to benefit from lower-priced feedstock, it is expected that these savings will be passed to consumers at the retail level in the form of lower gasoline pump prices. The industry has said that and it is generally acknowledged. I hear Hon. Members opposite scoffing.

The Government also expects that Petro-Canada, as one of those companies, will act in a responsible manner in competing with other oil companies in the market-place. Furthermore, deregulation has answered that Canada's oil market is fully open to the forces of international competition. Most regions of the country are exposed to oil product imports from the United States and overseas. These imports help to keep Canadian oil product prices in line with those in international markets. The recent rapid decline in oil product prices could force Canadian oil product price redutions even before refiners benefit from lower crude oil costs. This is what free market forces are all about.
Here endeth the lesson: The motion to have the Government force Petro-Canada to lower its pump prices by six cents per litre is both unnecessary and unrealistic. The Government no longer finances Petro-Canada; and it certainly does not get involved in the day-to-day operations of Crown corporations. Government interference of this sort risks doing serious damage not only to Petro-Canada but also the Canadian oil industry which provides thousands of jobs throughout the country.
I conclude by reminding the House that the Government is committed to deregulation. This means allowing market forces to operation without Government interference. None of us want a return to the oppressive Liberal-NDP regime of regulation, the legacy of which is our national debt and our overweening deficit.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 63-PRICE OF GASOLINE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the Hon. Member two questions. He reiterated again the usual Conservative argument that it was the NDP which created the tremendous difficulties for the industry. The United States has the most progressive Government that country has had in the last 50 years. A year or two ago Exxon, which invested between $2 billion and $3 billion to build a plant which would extract oil from shale, I believe in Colorado, closed down its operation. The Americans did not have a national energy program. Why did they close this operation down? They did so because the idea of building that plant was based on a very high-priced barrel of oil. Why did they do the same thing as companies did in Canada, when they did not have a national energy program to worry about?
The second question I wish to ask the Hon. Member is this. He suggests that when we propose a specific reduction in price, this is a Marxist idea and interferes with the free market. Can the Hon. Member explain why it is that Conservative provincial Governments in Ontario, Saskatchewan and Alberta operate marketing boards for milk, eggs and hogs, the purpose of which is to help producers and to put in place a price floor which interferes with the market? Is that not a Marxist idea as well, just to use the Hon. Member's thinking on the subject?
Or is this the case because that is the only way in which industries can survive?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 63-PRICE OF GASOLINE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have been asked those questions by the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North. First, with respect to the question of the closing down of the shale project in, and I believe he is right, it may be Colorado or Wyoming, there is a distinct difference between the American situation and the Canadian situation. That is to say that the United States decision was made not because the Government was pro-business or anti-business but simply because the people of the United States have the good common sense not to tax to its knees an industry which is an engine of growth.
With respect to the question of helping producers and the objectives of marketing boards, we are hearing a contradiction from the Hon. Member opposite. The NDP line is that we are giving money to oil companies. Yet, I hear the Hon. member for Winnipeg North saying that the purpose of marketing boards is to help producers. Who in heaven's name are the producers if they are not those same invidious and malicious oil companies, be they domestic or international?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 63-PRICE OF GASOLINE

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 63-PRICE OF GASOLINE

Obviously, then, no onw would invest in the energy industry, and Imperial, Gulf and Shell would have done poorly in Canada all these years. This is the old canard of the industry. It constantly asks about the rate of return. It is the figures provided by the industry that count. It counts as part of its investment the oil in the ground, which does not belong to it. February 4, 1986

Petroleum Association as reflected in the report to the monitoring agency.
1 want to ask the Hon. Member two short questions. I have made the case today for a market which is not free. The Hon. Member is a free marketer. Surely, if he looks at the Bertrand Report, the Work of the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission, the evidence we have heard from small independent dealers, and at the fact that 70 per cent of the retail industry is controlled by four oil companies, would he not admit that we do not really have a free market? Second, I would like to know what position the Hon. Member took on the expansion of Petro-Canada when the Government bought the gas stations from Gulf, that is, his own personal position.

The fact is that if we had an NDP Government, which God forbid, we would have a marvellous conglomerate ridden with corruption and inefficiencies. We would have a nationalized oil industry in total.
Finally, there is the marvellous tendency-proclivity I might say-of the New Democrats to ride two horses, to want to have it both ways.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S O. 63-PRICE OF GASOLINE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have a chance to speak in this debate on the pricing of petroleum products and Petro-Canada because it is an issue of great concern in practically every riding in this country. People see the headlines every day and know that crude oil prices are dropping from $28 or $29 a barrel in U.S. funds to $18 a
Supply
barrel, which is a 33 per cent drop or more, and they are wondering why gasoline prices are not going down at the pumps.
I have a selection of headlines which appeared during the last couple of days. I think that from them we can get some feeling of the problems the Government faces with this issue. For instance, on February 1, the headline in The Ottawa Citizen read: "Federal Energy Policy in Confusion". On January 27 the headline in the Montreal Gazette read: "Customers' Revolt Brewing Over High Gasoline Prices". In the Chronicle Herald on January 23, the headline read: "Gas Tax Bite Too High, Canadian Automobile Association Says". The Ottawa Citizen headline on January 24 read: "Tourism Officials Want Pump Prices to Reflect World Price Cut". The headline in the Toronto Star on January 24 read: "Why is Our Oil Price So High? Industry Has Few Answers". In the Toronto Star of January 23, the headline read: "Excess Gas Prices Cost $8.5 Million Each Day". In the Montreal Gazette on the same day the headline read: "Wilson Won't Lower PetroCan's Gas Prices". On January 22nd, the Toronto Star headline read: "We Could Wait Months Before Gasoline Prices Drop, Minister of Energy Carney Says". That is the consumer side of the issue. In the Montreal Gazette on January 22, the headline read: "Oil Prices Continue to Fall but Not at the Gas Pumps". In the Toronto Sun on January 20 the headline read: "Rip-Off at the Pumps", and there followed a detailed account.
Looking back a little further we see another headline: "PetroCan Names Moore Firm as Consultants", and it goes into great detail about how $100,000 is being paid for consultant fees to Frank Moore to advise PetroCan. Obviously, he has not advised them as yet to lower prices. And as we search through the article we see his cohorts in that advisory group. Mr. Doucette, the brother of the senior aide of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), headed up a company which lost $20 million in East Coast energy. We can then understand why there is difficulty in PetroCan getting the policy right.
Going back a few months to the cut-back in the Petroleum Incentives Program, we see the headline: "Frontier Oil Rigs to be Cut, Analyst Predicts". A little farther back from last year we see: "Promise of Offshore Oil Fading in Nova Scotia", and "PetroCan Plans Gas Station Closures. Small Explorers Ponder Future". That was back on November 1, 1985, at the time of the new energy agreements. I have here a very forthright article written by the President of PetroCan in the Toronto Star on January 25. The headline reads: "PetroCan Chief Speaks Out on Painful Lay-offs and Closings of PetroCan Gas Stations". Here is another headline: "Low Oil Prices Worry PetroCan Chief'.
With respect to the motion before us today. I would like to speak briefly about the adverse impact of the oil price drop and the Government's lack of policy with regard to it. I also want to talk about the impact of the oil price reduction and the lack of action taken by the Government over the last year to take economic advantage of lower oil prices. For instance, it is not only the national price of oil, as we would see in metropolitan areas such as Toronto, but it is the impact we see in the

February 4, 1986
Supply
more remote areas of our country. Sault Ste. Marie is a medium-sized city serving an area with 120,000 people. It is quite a distance from Metropolitan Toronto. Regular gasoline currently is selling in Sault Ste. Marie at about 54 cents a litre compared to about 61 cents a litre in Toronto, which works out to a difference of seven cents a litre. If we compare that with the population, we find that the resident population consumes about 71 million litres of gasoline per year. That price difference means that the residents of Sault Ste. Marie have to pay around $5 million more a year. For an average family driving an average number of miles, that adds up to an extra cost of $150 a year. If they drive across the bridge to Sault Ste. Marie, Michigan, they will save at least $10 a tank of gas.
We have to ask ourselves whether Petro-Canada, when it was established in the mid-1970s, was meant to be a window on the industry or a bank vault for the Government. On June 1 last, Petro-Canada spent tens of thousands of dollars for advertisements to say it was bringing down the price of gasoline at the pump. The company placed an ad in The Sault Star on June 1, 1985 which said that Petro-Canada was pleased to announce lower prices at the pump. The company said that the recent federal Budget changed the levies on petroleum products and it was pleased to pass on those cost reductions to its customers. Due to decontrol, the company said, and removal of the Canadian ownership special charge, Petro-Canada is lowering the posted price of products such as gasoline and diesel fuel by six-tenths of a cent per litre. Heating fuel was reduced by one-half cent per litre. The prices were effective June 1 at all company-operated and agency stations. That, of course, was very good. The actual petroleum compensation charge was 1.8 cents a litre and they only passed on a portion, six-tenths of a cent per litre, but at least they did something.
