speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Parliamentary Secretary knows that the petroleum compensation charge put in effect in November, 1984 was 1.8 cents per litre.
This advertisement shows that the Government can give leadership if it wants to. That is what Canadians are calling on the Government to do. They want Petro-Canada to give leadership. I am sure Petro-Canada did not dream up this campaign itself. It probably did it at the suggestion or behest of the Minister. The company is capable of giving leadership on prices, and that is what Members of this House are asking it to do today.
In a front page article in The Sault Star, the Federation of Northern Ontario Municipalities demanded a monitoring
system to track gasoline prices and try to bring some relationship between the prices in northern and southern Ontario. As I pointed out, people in the North are very concerned at the additional cost they have to pay. They have longer distances to travel for health care, shopping and things like that. I received a letter from a couple living in Elliott Lake, Mr. and Mrs. E. A. Smith. They said they are being hurt by the high price of gasoline. They are pensioners and they have to watch every cent they spend. When they look at making a trip to visit their family in Nova Scotia, possibly for the last time, they are looking at a lot of money for gas. They ask why it is that the U.S. gas is so much cheaper than ours. "Why can our gas not be reduced to a reasonable level so we can afford to drive our car rather than to have it sit in the driveway until the pension cheque comes in?" That is very typical of letters that Members on all sides receive. I am sure the Parliamentary Secretary and other Members on the Government side are getting the same kind of letters. I have another letter from the English Tea House in Desbarats, Ontario. Mr. Johnstone protests the very high price of fuel, not only gasoline. He points out that the price of propane has gone up dramatically from 27 cents to 32 cents a litre. This may not seem like a very large increase between 1984 and 1986, but when you go to fill a 500-gallon tank for a senior citizen like this it is very expensive. He points out at the same time that he uses kerosene for spot heaters and that the price of kerosene has gone up from 51 cents a litre to 56 cents a litre or $2.55 a gallon in one year. This is a tremendous hardship. It was at a time when oil prices were supposedly deregulated, the world price was falling by several dollars a barrel, and of course it has fallen dramatically since. This is the kind of concern being expressed.
I would also like to talk about the anguish that Petro-Canada dealers have to go through. Even though they own all of the gasoline and fuel oil in their tanks, they are forced by contract to sell at a price that Petro-Canada dictates to them. We have an example of that in Bracebridge, Ontario. The company has a formula, which means that the more you charge, the higher your commission. For example, at 55.9 cents a litre you get a commission of 3.4 cents. If you only charge 47.9 cents a litre, you only get 2.8 cents. This is from a pricing schedule for Petro-Canada's Trafalgar terminal as of September 3, 1985. As of January 1, 1986, the company escalated the price at which you get the maximum commission from 55.9 cents to 58.4 cents, but the commission is the same. The whole commission arrangement is designed not to sell more gasoline but to charge a higher price. The dealer who gave me this information is very upset. He feels that the company is totally ruthless, uncaring, and unfair in its relationships.
That is one aspect of the situation as I see it today. The other aspect of the Western Accord and the policy of the Government is that there is very little provision in the Western Accord to maintain and keep the oil industry functioning in a healthy state in western Canada when oil prices are falling. As a matter of fact, the only provision for that in the Western
February 4, 1986

Accord is Section 9 which reads: "In the event of international oil marketing disturbances that result in short-changes to crude oil prices with potentially negative impacts on Canada, the Government of Canada, following consultations with provincial Governments, will take appropriate measures to protect Canadian interests."
We are already seeing that in spades, Mr. Speaker. Besides that policy, which is very inadequate to deal with the rapid drop in crude oil prices, we are already seeing major projects falling like tenpins across Canada. There is no adequate provision in that agreement to deal with price drops to $18, $15, or $12 a barrel.
I recently spoke with an exploration company which said that when the price of crude oil drops to $20 a barrel it cuts its exploration program in half. If the price drops more, its exploration program will be reduced more. Many projects have either been cancelled or are at a standstill. The $4 billion Suncrude oil sands project is under the gun and certainly cannot go forward with this pricing regime. Also affected are the new oil sands plant of Petro-Canada, the phased expansion of the heavy oil up-grading programs at Cold Lake and Wolf Lake, and the $3.2 billion Husky Oil up-grader at Lloydminster.
I had a chance to visit that plant last May with a number of my caucus colleagues. It seemed to me that that was a model project which could have been self-sufficient and created a large number of jobs. Yet, the Government was obviously already sending signals to the company last summer that it was calling the project into question and was starting to draw back from the $50 commitment of the former Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. Of course, the $750 million loan guarantee is falling by the wayside. It was a model project which could have been very beneficial.
Last week the $2.3 billion liquefied natural gas project in Prince Rupert was cancelled. Other projects are on hold and very uncertain. There is not much chance that the 300,000 jobs which were promised by the Minister will be created. That is mostly due to the fact that this agreement has no provision in it to deal with rapid price losses.
It is obvious that consumers of the country want the drop in world oil prices to be passed through to them. It seems to me that the Government's whole energy policy is in doubt with regard to whether the jobs will be created, whether the massive projects will go ahead, and whether we are going to be able to achieve and maintain the self-sufficiency which we enjoyed for the last couple of years in oil production.

That this House demands that the Government instruct Petro-Canada and its retail outlets to reduce their prices at the pump by six cents a litre, a move which would enable Petro-Canada to fulfil one of its basic purposes which is to provide Canada with reasonable energy prices.
I have no hesitation in supporting that motion and 1 take particular pleasure in having the opportunity to conclude the debate on this motion this afternoon.
The situation that faces Canadians and the Government as well is very simple. Canadians have lived for years with rising petroleum prices, including the price of gasoline at the pump and heating fuel for homes. At present they see that the international petroleum price is dropping sharply with all kinds of consequence. Those Canadians expect those decreases to be obvious to them at the pump. However, they find that in January the prices are rising.

There are many reasons to doubt the very market forces in which the Parliamentary Secretary has put his faith. There is good reason for my friend from Vancouver-Kingsway to put forward a motion asking the Government to intervene with the publicly owned oil company, which is not only our window on the industry but a vehicle by which to ensure that something remotely resembling market forces will prevail in Canadian petroleum.
All Members of the House recognize this problem as our constituents write to us about the difficulty they have in enjoying the use of their automobile for driving to work or enjoying their retirement. This was a concern of one of my constituents who wrote to me recently. In fact, he wrote to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Miss Carney), asking how he and his

The Government is eager to raise more money through regressive forms of taxation such as sales tax increases and increases in the price of fuel, without coming to grips with other issues. The Parliamentary Secretary said that we have no program to describe how we would raise revenue. If he paid attention to our fair taxation program he would know that we have an answer. It is bad enough that the cost of gasoline should rise because the Government has slapped some more taxation on ordinary Canadians. The price of heating fuel is 40 cents a litre in Thunder Bay. I asked my assistants to check on the taxes that are involved in that 40 cents a litre for heating oil. They told me there is not a cent of tax in that. I am paying 56 cents a litre for unleaded gasoline. Constituents of mine who cannot use natural gas or electricity are paying 40 cents a litre for heating oil and there is no tax on it. My God, Mr. Speaker, what are we to say about the oil companies that are supposedly-

The argument of the Parliamentary Secretary is based on the proposition that market forces should prevail. The petroleum industry is not an industry in which market forces are anything remotely resembling neoclassical economic theory or principles of atavistic competition. Nothing remotely resembling that existed in the petroleum industry for years past. To depend on market forces to do what is required to bring prices down is pursuing will-o'-the-wisp.
First, we all know, even though these friends of ours on the other side do not talk about it, that the price of petroleum

reached the levels it did in the last 15 years because of a cartel. The most spectacularly successful cartel in human history drove the price of petroleum from $3 a barrel to $38 and more.

speechtext:
Take that in percentage terms and consider the impact and the transfer of wealth that was carried out thanks to the existence of the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries.
The question that all Canadian Governments faced in the late 1970s and into the 1980s as they contemplated the operations of the cartel which, under its price-setting umbrella, sheltered the seven sisters of the oil industry and their operations in Canada as they drew out of the pockets of Canadian consumers enormous quantities of money, was whether they should take it and run. They could have done so so easily if left to what is called market forces, but Canadian Governments decided they should not.
The remarkable thing is that when the petroleum and gas revenue tax was imposed, the oil companies did not suffer particularly. If one takes the statistics of that development, it is astonishing to realize that the industry's share of revenues in 1980 was $6.3 billion, in 1981 it rose to $6.7 billion, in 1982 to $9.4 billion and in 1983 to $10.6 billion. Is that an industry that is hurting?
From 1982 and 1983, Imperial Oil had an increase in profits from $289 million to $344 million.

The Government, by repealing the petroleum and gas revenue tax, has given all of that money back to the oil companies. Now we have the decline of OPEC's power. But are those market forces of the neoclassical economic theory? They are nothing of the sort. What my friend has sought particularly to deal with is the reality of a handful of petroleum companies which control the industry, determine prices, and set prices at the pump. They set prices at the pump because they have the power to determine at what price gasoline will be sold. Anyone interested in the topic of combinations of economic power exerted in the market-place is aware that retail price maintenance has been one of the most contentious principles over the years. Governments have attempted to come to grips with that problem. In the oil industry there is no doubt about it. It is perfectly obvious that the people running the stations and selling the gas are under the control of the companies from which they buy gasoline or from whom they receive it on consignment. Retail price maintenance in the purist sense is what Petro-Canada and the rest are involved in. Market forces Mr. Speaker? Do not make me laugh. When we have a

situation of four or five companies in an oligopoly, we do not have anything like an atavistic response to millions of consumers, we have several companies involved in establishing prices and maintaining them.
In this context of that kind of market power being exercised by a few companies, companies will now, thanks to what the Government has done, take far more of the gains they can get. After all, we are talking about $20 a barrel. We are not yet down to $5 or $6. We might conceivably get there but we are still a long way from that.
The Government, which is supposedly concerned about the prosperity of all Canada and ordinary Canadians, is letting the companies take the gains. It hopes devoutly this money will be sunk into exploration and that it will generate the 300,000 jobs, but the Government has not given us a guarantee of that.
This is revenue the Government needs so desperately which the Minister of Finance will invoke when he brings in his Budget. The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) has to admit that this revenue was the reason for his promise of last January to maintain the value in the child benefits package. It is strange that the Government could do that to mothers and babies and at the same time give hundreds of millions it not billions of dollars to the oil companies and then talk to us about market forces. These are brute economic realities which the Government does not want to admit to.

Mr. Speaker, I wanted to rise this evening in response to a question that I put to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) with regard to the subject matter of free trade. At that time I raised the issue as it affects cultural industries. The main thrust of the subject matter of free trade concerns me greatly. I have been asked on numerous occasions as to whether or not I am in support of the Mulroney initiative as it relates to free trade.
Unfortunately, with the way in which the Government has conducted itself to date, I would have to say that I am opposed to the Mulroney initiative with regard to free trade. That is not to suggest in any way that as a Member of Parliament I am opposed to the concept of free trade. As a Member of Parliament, I find it somewhat appalling and extremely difficult when the Government of the day says a whole lot about free trade, the various platitudes, but fails to provide Canadians with the necessary information as to the direction in which it will take our country.
Yes, Canada has a surplus with the United States of about $21 billion in free trade, and we are to sit down with the United States and negotiate an improved a deal. What we do not know with regard to free trade is the cost benefit to the various sectors of the economy. I had hoped that the Government would have laid before Parliament how free trade will benefit my Province of Nova Scotia and the Atlantic region.
We can go back to 1933 when the former Premier of Nova Scotia, Angus L. Macdonald initiated a study which showed the objections that that Government had with regard to the tariff policy of Sir John A. Macdonald. We have no information from this Government. What we have is bits and pieces of information as they relate to brewery workers in my province,
February 4, 1986

textile workers in Truro, Nova Scotia, and how it will affect them. No cost benefit study has been done, or if it has been done, it has been in secret. We have to know whether regional economic development incentive programs are on the chopping block or the negotiating table.
What about unemployment insurance? Is that, too, going to be on the negotiating table when we sit down with our good friends in the United States? What about the various fishery programs, Mr. Speaker? We have a decision here of late from the United States regarding programs which have been determined to provide subsidies. Are they going to be a part of the negotiating apparatus with the United States? Will federal programs such as the fishing vessel assistance program, the agricultural and rural development agreements, the federal Department of Fisheries and Oceans Promotions Branch, the federal Economic and Regional Development Agreements Program, assistance for the construction of ice-making and fish chilling facilities and the fishing vessel insurance plan be up for negotiation? We do not have an answer. In Newfoundland there are grants for purchasing and constructing boats. Will that be on the negotiating table? Will the Newfoundland loan guarantees from the Fisheries Loan Board be up for negotiation? Will the Nova Scotia fishing vessels construction program and the Nova Scotia industrial development division grants from the Department of Development be on the negotiating table with our friends, the Americans? What about the assistance for ice-making and fish-chilling facilities in Prince Edward Island?
There has been a vacuum when it comes to good, precise information on the whole subject of free trade. I cannot see why the Government, if it believes strongly in its assertion that free trade will benefit Canada and the regions, would not provide that information willingly to Hon. Members of Parliament and the provincial Governments. With regard to the free trade issue, conceptually it does have some benefits. The liberalization of trade, not only in the United States but other countries of the world as well, has been the position of my Party for quite some time.
Where is the information? Where are the concrete cost benefit analyses? Why have they not been done? If they have been done, why have they not been provided so that we can have a serious, intelligent debate on the subject which is germane to economic development in my region? I would hope that the Parliamentary Secretary could avail himself of this opportunity to provide Canadians with an answer as to why that information has not been made readily available. Without this information, the Government is asking Members of Parliament to make decisions prematurely without having all the information and facts before them.
I have listed for your information, Mr. Speaker, a number of programs which have been deemed by the United States to be the equivalent of subsidies. Are they now going to be part and parcel of the negotiating process? I would hope that we would get a clear answer from the Government of Canada and
Adjournment Debate
hopefully from the Government of Nova Scotia. However, we know that the Government of Nova Scotia is not too wise when it comes to doing cost benefit analyses. It is prepared to agree to anything put forward by the Government of Canada, something which I think is a mistake.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, that is quite an indictment of the Nova Scotia Government. It signed an energy agreement with the Government to which the Hon. Member once belonged. I am sure that when he re-examines his words-
I'm talking about free trade.

If you stick to the subject.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
-and we had to bear seven minutes of his tirade.
It has been very clear for some time that the Government wants a better, more predictable and more secure trading relationship with our major trading partners so that Canadian enterprise can plan, invest and grow with confidence, the kind of confidence that leads to more and better jobs. Of particular interest is the United States market which now takes three-quarters of our total exports. What will be involved in this? These will be commercial negotiations between two distinct and sovereign countries. We all know that modern nations are more than economic. The challenge will be to strengthen both our economy and our sovereignty.
We and the Americans will be working toward a package of mutually beneficial and acceptable reductions in tariff and non-tariff barriers in order to increase trade and thereby save jobs and create new jobs in the future. In order to get a good deal, each side will have to be prepared to listen to the other. We want the Americans to consider our concerns about the protectionist effect of their trade remedy legislation, our desire to gain greater access to their government procurement market and the need for a more effective and predictable way to settle our differences.
The Americans will want us to listen to their concerns about our high tariffs, our industrial support programs, our investment rules and the international rules regarding trade in services. By listening to each other and placing these concerns on the table, neither side is committed to accepting what the other is proposing. However, only by frankly discussing each other's objectives and concerns will we know if a good deal is possible. We are prepared to do that. As the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) indicated in his announcement of September 26, if a deal which is good for all regions and all Canadians is not negotiable, there will be no deal.

February 4, 1986
Adjournment Debate
1 might add that I think Canadians do not appreciate having to go to the United States, cap in hand, when each individual issue comes up, whether it be an issue with respect to wood, steel or fisheries. They do not appreciate having to go down there and say: "Please, do not include us in your tariff or in your protectionist Bills". I think the Canadian people want us to negotiate a fair trade agreement with the United States. We are prepared to do that. If it is not a fair deal, and if it is not good for Canadians, then we will not sign it.

subtopic: ATOMIC ENERGY OF CANADA LIMITED-RADIOACTIVE WASTE DISPOSAL RESEARCH. (B) UNITED STATES DUMP SITE
ATOMIC ENERGY OF CANADA LIMITED-RADIOACTIVE WASTE DISPOSAL RESEARCH. (B) UNITED STATES DUMP SITE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to follow up on a question I asked of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Miss Carney) on January 27 last. I suppose the Minister of Energy is so used to hearing me ask questions in which I seek assurances that the site of AECL's underground research laboratory at Lac du Bonnet, Manitoba, will not become the eventual site for a Canadian radioactive garbage dump that when I got up to ask the question she did not pay all that much attention to it. She must have assumed I was asking the same question I have asked repeatedly. She went on to say that she had given assurances to the Manitoba Government that the AECL research site would not become a permanent site for radioactive waste disposal. However, that is not the question I asked.
I asked a question about the concern expressed by the Manitoba Government, and by others, about the list of potential American radioactive dump sites which was recently released. I asked her whether or not in view of the fact that many of those sites, if they were to be used, might have an effect on waters entering Canada-in particular, groundwater-she would consider instructing AECL not to enter into any further agreements with the U.S. Department of Energy for co-operating in research which is taking place at the Lac du Bonnet site. I am thinking particularly of those waters which are adjacent to the Red River Basin.
The reason I asked her the question is I think that we have a very good bargaining tool here insofar as the U.S. Department of Energy wants to participate in the research which is going on in Lac du Bonnet. My position is that we should say to the Americans: "Fine, if you want to use a Canadian site for research, then part of the price for being able to use that site is that you take off the list of potential American sites those sites which might affect Canadian watersheds". In my view this would give the Government some leverage with the Americans with respect to the issue of sites which might potentially damage Canada.
I might also say that this might be something which would be looked upon favourably by the people of Minnesota who have been successful, as I understand it, in preventing the American Department of Energy from carrying on in Minnesota the type of research that AECL is carrying on in Manitoba. By allowing the U.S. Department of Energy to do
research in Lac du Bonnet we are effectively allowing it to circumvent the successful opposition which has been generated in Minnesota. Because the rock formations are similar, and by being able to conduct research in Lac du Bonnet, the U.S. Department of Energy is able to do an end run around the opposition in Minnesota and do the very type of research which, depending on what is found, might lead to the selection of the very sites in Minnesota with which we are concerned.
I say to the Government: Take this opportunity of leverage and instruct AECL not to co-operate any further with the U.S. Department of Energy until such time as those sites which potentially could affect Canada are removed from the American list. I might add that it is not just a question of responding favourably to the concerns of people in Minnesota. It is also the quite simple question of not co-operating, not helping people to dirty our own backyard or, in this case, dirty our groundwater and our watersheds. It is also a question of the extent to which, by co-operating with the U.S. Department of Energy, we involve ourselves in the whole American nuclear program. This waste does not all come from reactors. The waste the Americans are looking to dispose of comes as well from their nuclear weapons program. I think that the extent we co-operate with the U.S. Department of Energy in an uncritical way in finding ways to dispose of this waste is the extent to which we should be collaborators, if you will, in the American nuclear program of which, as we all know, many Canadians are critical.
I see this partnership that AECL has entered into with the U.S. Department of Energy vis-a-vis the underground research laboratory in Lac du Bonnet, Manitoba, as one more way in which Canada has become integrated into the whole American nuclear program. I regret that very much. For that reason, to be honest, I would be against co-operating with the Americans in an uncritical way even if these sites in Minnesota had not been released recently.
I say to those whose opposition to this may be more qualified that mine that this is another reason for bargaining toughly with the Americans about the ways in which we co-operate with them. At the very least, the Government should be now saying to the Americans: "Listen. Until you take those sites off the list, those in Minnesota and elsewhere, which could potentially affect Canada, we cannot possibly hope to co-operate any further". Otherwise, we could be open to the accusation that we were helping the Americans pollute our own backyard, and that is not acceptable to us.

subtopic: TRADE-REMOVAL OF TARIFF ON COMPUTER PARTS
TRADE-REMOVAL OF TARIFF ON COMPUTER PARTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, you are aware, as I am, that ever since the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the Government announced last September that they desired to enter into trade negotiations with the United States, the issue has been discussed very, very widely across this country. The issue has entailed a debate and discussions relating to the whole question of our negotiations or nonnegotiations with the U.S.; the possibility of extending those negotiations right around the world to our other trading partners through the General Agreement on Trade and Tariffs, otherwise known as GATT; the whole question of tariffs, their removal, and non-tariff barriers and their removal.
In light of all those discussions, it came as quite a surprise to me that on January 20 the Government announced it was removing our own tariff barrier on computer parts. One would have thought that perhaps that tariff would have been part of the trade discussions which went on in a general way with the U.S. or our other trading partners through the GATT discussions. So, as I said, it was a surprise, at least to me, when the Government announced these tariff barriers were being removed.
This was particularly significant in my own constituency because located there is what is really the original home of IBM Canada. I suppose one might have described that as the typical American branch plant in Canada but it has gone far beyond that. There is now a considerable number of IBM plants in Canada. Even in my own riding, while we have I suppose the biggest IBM production centre, there are a number of other plants. They employ in my own constituency somewhere around 3,000 workers. About 2,000 are engaged in the manufacture of computer parts and the other thousand are engaged in computer research. I would venture to say that if there is an area involving the leading edge of computer technology, it is probably located right in my constituency in those IBM plants. Obviously, anything which impacts on their profitability is going to be of significance to my particular constituency and, indeed, to Canada itself.
It is interesting to note that although at one time, I suppose, those IBM plants manufactured complete lines of computers, they now specialize in particular parts of computers. Those plants have from IBM International a world product mandate for particular computer parts. They compete with other IBM plants around the world for the right to manufacture certain parts for computers. They export those parts right around the world. As a result, I am told, the export trade on their part is growing at the rate of about 20 per cent each year. That is a substantial trade for Canada and obviously for the company itself.

February 4, 1986
Adjournment Debate
IBM is most interested in the whole area of trade negotiations, and particularly in the concept of tariff reduction. It is interested in the discussions with the United States because it sees some opportunities there to expand and further its own export markets. It is interested in the across-the-board negotiations which the Government is in fact proposing. I am told by the executives at IBM that they were most concerned about the approach that the former Government took with sectoral trade negotiations, but that they welcome the idea of across-the-board negotiations.
Therefore, it is particularly significant when we find that the 3.9 per cent tariff on Canadian computer parts has now been abandoned. It was as a result of that that I expressed my concern as to whether we were getting some comparable trade concessions from other countries. IBM and other Canadian computer parts manufacturers have to export and compete in foreign markets and, obviously, are interested in having the tariffs reduced.
At the same time, I was interested and asked the Minister what the impact would be on our computer industry, particularly on IBM, of dropping that particular tariff barrier. When I asked that question on January 27 the Minister assured me that the tariff barrier that was being removed was also being removed in Japan and in the United States. I was pleased to hear that. I did not get from the Minister the actual impact that it could have on our industry and on the computer industry in my riding in particular.
I hope that the Parliamentary Secretary will have some information tonight as to what that impact will be because the Government has computer models to indicate what impact that sort of tariff reduction will have on particular sectors. I would be most interested to hear that from the Parliamentary Secretary tonight.

speakeroldname: Mr. John McDermid (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: TRADE-REMOVAL OF TARIFF ON COMPUTER PARTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in response to the comments made by the Hon. Member for York East (Mr. Redway) concerning the elimination of our tariffs on computer parts, I would first like to give a little history to indicate how this came about.
During the Quebec Summit the Prime Minister (Mr. Mul-roney) and the President of the United States directed that action be undertaken to resolve specific impediments to trade. One of the areas to be examined was the feasibility of mutual elimination of tariffs on high technology goods including computers, computer parts, and semiconductors. At the same time, the U.S. and Japan were examining ways to improve two-way trade in high technology products and Canada was asked to join with those two countries in removing tariffs on computer parts and semiconductors. In fact, the U.S. and Japan eliminated tariffs on semiconductors on March 1, 1985.
The Department of Finance undertook a review of this issue, including a survey of Canadian manufacturers of computers,
computer parts, and semiconductors. Almost all respondents, including IBM which is in the Hon. Member's constituency, and which I have had the pleasure of touring a couple of times-is a great plant-expressed strong support for reciprocal elimination of tariffs on these products. The desire on the part of Canadian computer manufacturers to have duty-free entry of computer parts and semiconductors is, of course, based on the fact that they have to import many of these articles and feel that free entry will enhance their competitiveness.
Although our industry is in favour of eliminating all tariffs on computers, computer parts, and semiconductors, the U.S. informed us that it was not prepared to remove its tariff protection on computers. In view of this, it was decided that Canada should not proceed in this area at this time.
The elimination of the Canadian tariffs on computer parts and semiconductors was effective, as the Hon. Member mentioned, January 20, 1986, and paralleled action taken by the United States on or shortly before that date to remove its duties on computer parts. Japan removed its tariffs on computer parts on January 20. By the way, it also took similar action on computers themselves.
Trade data for 1984 show that imports of computer parts amounted to about $1.1 billion of which $1 billion was from the U.S. and $16 million from Japan. About $1.3 billion of semiconductors were imported in 1984. Of these only $25 million worth were subject to duty. In the same year, our exports of computer parts were valued at about $300 million, most of which went to the United States. Semiconductor exports were valued at $565 million, of which $497 million went to the United States and $4 million to Japan. These statistics show that while our imports of computer parts are far in excess of our exports of these products, the tariff elimination on semiconductors provides a more balanced package of concessions.
I might say that representatives of IBM and other members of the Canadian Business Equipment Manufacturers Association recently met with Finance officials and expressed their complete satisfaction with the action taken by the Government. They see the removal of these tariffs as benefiting their industry by reducing the cost of components they import for their manufacturing operations and by increasing the opportunity to penetrate the United States and Japanese markets.
In conclusion, we believe that this tariff elimination is an important step in demonstrating Canada's strong commitment to trade liberalization and represents a positive follow-up to the Quebec summit.
